title: Why Doctors Refused to Wash Their Hands
description:
In 1846 Vienna, mothers begged not to be taken through one hospital door. Professor Ved follows Ignaz Semmelweis like a detective: two maternity clinics with very different death rates, the suspects he ruled out, the autopsy accident that cracked the case, the chlorine bowl that cut deaths about tenfold, why medicine still said no (and the fair reasons it had), how germ theory proved him right, and the 'Semmelweis reflex' that still trips us up today.

Sources: Semmelweis's clinic figures (via Wikipedia and Britannica); Carson & Toodayan, 'Ignaz Philipp Semmelweis: herald of hygienic medicine', Medical Journal of Australia (2018); Britannica, 'Verification of the germ theory'; WHO, first global report on infection prevention and control (6 May 2022). Reconstructions are illustrations, not archival footage.
speaker: ved

scenes.say: Vienna, eighteen forty-six. A young mother arrives at one of the biggest hospitals in Europe... and begs, on her knees, not to be taken through one particular door.
Because everyone in the city knew: behind that door, mothers died. And the reason was hiding in plain sight... on the doctors' own hands.
This is the story of the doctor who worked it out, why almost nobody believed him, and why the hardest thing to wash off... isn't germs.
The Vienna General Hospital had two maternity clinics, side by side. The First Clinic trained doctors and medical students. The Second trained midwives.

layers.title: Vienna General Hospital
layers.sub: 1846. The First Clinic: doctors and medical students

scenes.say: In eighteen forty-six, the First Clinic lost *eleven point four percent* of its mothers to childbed fever. The Second Clinic? About *two point eight*.

layers.title: FIRST CLINIC
layers.text:
Doctors and medical students.
1846: 4,010 births, 459 mothers died.
SOURCE: SEMMELWEIS'S CLINIC TABLES, VIA WIKIPEDIA

scenes.say: Same city. Same building. Mothers from the same streets. And about *four times* the deaths, just for going through the wrong door.
So mothers begged to be sent to the Second Clinic. Some would rather give birth in the street on the way in. And strangely... those street births rarely caught the fever.
A street was safer than a hospital. That should have set off every alarm in medicine.

layers.text:
Hospital review: 1 star.
The street was cleaner.

scenes.say: One young doctor couldn't let it go. Ignaz Semmelweis, a Hungarian assistant in the First Clinic. He treated the deaths like a crime... and went through the suspects one by one.
Overcrowding? No. The Second Clinic was *more* crowded.

layers.title: SUSPECT 1: OVERCROWDING
layers.text: The Second Clinic was MORE crowded.

scenes.say: The weather, or bad city air? Both clinics sat in the same hospital, breathing the same air.

layers.title: SUSPECT 1: OVERCROWDING
layers.text: The Second Clinic was MORE crowded.

scenes.say: The way mothers lay to give birth? He changed it in the First Clinic. The deaths didn't change.

layers.title: SUSPECT 1: OVERCROWDING
layers.text: The Second Clinic was MORE crowded.

layers.title: SUSPECT 3: BIRTH POSITION
layers.text: Changed it in the First Clinic. No effect.

scenes.say: He even wondered whether the priest, ringing a bell on his way to the dying, was frightening mothers to death. Every suspect had an alibi.
Then, in eighteen forty-seven, a tragedy cracked the case. His friend, Professor Jakob Kolletschka, was poked by a student's scalpel during an autopsy.
Soon after, Kolletschka was dead. And the illness that killed him looked just like the fever that was killing the mothers.
And Semmelweis saw it.
Doctors and students started their mornings in the autopsy room. Then they walked straight to the maternity ward, and examined mothers with the same hands. Midwives never did autopsies.

layers.title: THE ROUTE
layers.text:
Autopsy -> no wash -> delivery ward.
Midwives: no autopsies.

scenes.say: He called it *cadaverous particles*. Something invisible, carried from the dead to the living, on doctors' hands.
So in mid-May, eighteen forty-seven, he put a bowl by the door. Chlorinated lime solution. Wash your hands in it before you touch a patient. Every time.
Why chlorine? Because it was the best thing he'd found for getting rid of the smell of the autopsy room. If the smell was gone, he reasoned, so was whatever caused it.
In April, *eighteen point three percent* of mothers in the First Clinic had died. Then the bowl arrived. June: *two point two*. July: *one point two*.
In the year that followed, there were even months with *no* deaths from the fever at all.
About ten times fewer deaths. From a bowl of water. You'd think they'd build him a statue.
Instead, many senior doctors pushed back. Some were insulted. A gentleman's hands, they felt, were clean.

layers.text: “Doctors are gentlemen, and gentlemen's hands are clean.”
ATTRIBUTED TO CHARLES MEIGS, PHILADELPHIA OBSTETRICIAN

scenes.say: But to be fair, they had reasons. Medicine then blamed disease on bad air and imbalances in the body. Germs weren't part of the picture yet. Semmelweis had a result... but no mechanism to explain it.

layers.title: THE DOCTORS' CASE
layers.text: Disease = bad air (miasma) and imbalance of the body's humours. No known germs. A result without a cause.

layers.title: SEMMELWEIS'S CASE
layers.text: 18.3% -> 1.2% after hand washing. Clear numbers. But WHY? No mechanism yet.

scenes.say: And he made it harder. His full book only came out in eighteen sixty-one. And he wrote furious open letters, calling his critics *murderers*.
In eighteen forty-nine, his post in Vienna wasn't renewed. He went home to Hungary.

layers.title: Vienna, 1849
layers.sub: his assistant's post is not renewed

scenes.say: And there, he did it again. At St. Rochus Hospital in Pest, from eighteen fifty-one to fifty-five, just eight mothers died out of nine hundred and thirty-three births. Under *one percent*.
But the fight wore him down. In eighteen sixty-five, his health and behaviour failing, he was taken to an asylum. Two weeks later he died, aged forty-seven... from an infected wound.
The kind of infection he'd spent his life fighting.
Science caught up only around the time he died. In the eighteen-sixties, Louis Pasteur showed that tiny living microbes cause fermentation and decay.
In eighteen sixty-seven, the surgeon Joseph Lister published his method of killing germs in wounds with carbolic acid.
And Robert Koch proved that one specific germ causes one specific disease, starting with anthrax in eighteen seventy-six.

layers.title: ROBERT KOCH, 1876
layers.text: Anthrax: one specific germ causes one specific disease.

layers.title: ROBERT KOCH, 1882
layers.text: Tuberculosis: he finds the bacterium behind it.

scenes.say: Germ theory finally gave Semmelweis the mechanism he never had. He was right. He just couldn't show why.
Today, there's a name for what happened to him. The *Semmelweis reflex*: the urge to reject new evidence, because it clashes with what everyone already believes.

And his lesson still isn't finished. The World Health Organization says that out of every hundred patients in acute-care hospitals, *seven* in richer countries and *fifteen* in poorer ones catch an infection there.

scenes.say: Where good hand hygiene and other simple practices are followed, the WHO says about *seventy percent* of those infections can be prevented.
So the next time a fact feels inconvenient, check the evidence... before the reflex.
Because the hardest thing to wash off... is *we've always done it this way*.

is *“we've always done it this way.”*
